results.claim: The Aurignacian period spans approximately 43,000–33,000 years ago
results.reason: Standard chronology for the Aurignacian technocomplex; consistent with Higham et al. (2012) and recent reviews (e.g., Higham 2011, PNAS; Teyssandier 2008).

results.quote: first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex to spread across most of Europe
results.claim: The Aurignacian is the first Upper Palaeolithic technocomplex to spread across most of Europe
results.reason: Widely accepted characterization in Paleolithic archaeology; the Aurignacian represents the first pan-European UP culture.

results.quote: ivory figurines and flutes were found in well-dated layers (Higham et al., 2012)
results.claim: Ivory figurines and flutes were found in well-dated layers at Hohle Fels and Geissenklösterle
results.reason: Higham et al. (2012) provides the radiocarbon chronology for Geissenklösterle; the figurines (Hohle Fels) and flutes (both sites) are from these dated Aurignacian layers. Conard et al. (2009) and Higham et al. (2012) together establish this.

results.quote: Hohle Fels female figurine, carved from mammoth ivory, is at least 35,000 years old (Conard, 2009)
results.claim: The Hohle Fels female figurine is at least 35,000 years old
results.reason: Conard (2009, Nature 459:248-252) reports the figurine from basal Aurignacian layers dated to ≥35,000 cal BP. Verified via Crossref.

results.quote: Repeated sequences of such marks have been read as possible notational or information-storage devices (McPherron et al., 2022)
results.claim: Repeated sequences of Aurignacian marks have been interpreted as possible notational or information-storage devices
results.reason: McPherron et al. (2022) is 'Machine learning, bootstrapping, null models, and why we are still not 100% sure which bone surface modifications were made by crocodiles' (J. Hum. Evol. 164:103071) — it concerns crocodile tooth marks on bones, NOT Aurignacian geometric signs or notational systems. This is an incorrect citation.
results.suggest: Replace with correct citation for notational interpretation of Paleolithic marks (e.g., d'Errico 1998, Marshack 1972, or more recent work on Paleolithic notation systems).

results.quote: their repertoires might differ between regions, as personal ornaments do (Vanhaeren & d'Errico, 2006)
results.claim: Personal ornament repertoires differ between regions in the Aurignacian
results.reason: Vanhaeren & d'Errico (2006, J. Archaeol. Sci. 33:1105-1128) demonstrates distinct regional ornament types across Aurignacian Europe. Verified via Crossref.

results.quote: SignBase v1.0 (Bentz et al., 2020) records 531 Aurignacian mobile objects from 65 sites in 13 countries
results.claim: SignBase v1.0 contains 531 Aurignacian mobile objects from 65 sites across 13 countries
results.reason: The paper's live code downloads SignBase v1.0 from figshare and reports these exact numbers. The dataset citation (Bentz et al. 2020, figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.12000018.v1) is verified.

results.quote: so a national difference may reflect the excavation and preservation history of a few sites
results.claim: National differences in sign repertoires may reflect excavation and preservation history of a few dominant sites
results.reason: This is a valid methodological caveat supported by the paper's own data (Vogelherd = 30% of German sample, Castanet = 13% of French). Consistent with known sampling biases in Paleolithic archaeology.

results.quote: so these few rare-sign contrasts do not yet show separate regional traditions
results.claim: The rare-sign contrasts do not demonstrate separate regional sign traditions
results.reason: Supported by the paper's own analysis showing high site concentration and small counts for rare signs. The conclusion appropriately qualifies the negative result.

results.claim: Higham et al. (2012) provides well-dated layers for Geissenklösterle
results.reason: Higham et al. (2012, J. Hum. Evol. 62:664-676) is explicitly a radiocarbon chronology paper for Geissenklösterle. Verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1016/j.jhevol.2012.03.003).

results.claim: Conard (2009) reports the Hohle Fels female figurine age as at least 35,000 years
results.reason: Conard (2009, Nature 459:248-252) reports the figurine from basal Aurignacian dated ≥35,000 cal BP. Verified via Crossref (DOI 10.1038/nature07995). Note: reference incorrectly cites journal as 'Science' instead of 'Nature' (see check_bib.json).

results.claim: McPherron et al. (2022) interprets repeated mark sequences as possible notational devices
results.reason: Same error as claim 5. McPherron et al. (2022) is about crocodile bone surface modifications, not Aurignacian marks or notational systems. The citation is completely mismatched.
results.suggest: Replace with appropriate citation for notational interpretation of Paleolithic geometric signs.

results.claim: Vanhaeren & d'Errico (2006) show personal ornament repertoires differ between Aurignacian regions
results.reason: Verified via Crossref: Vanhaeren & d'Errico (2006, J. Archaeol. Sci. 33:1105-1128) demonstrates regional variation in Aurignacian personal ornaments.

results.claim: Dutkiewicz et al. (2020) created SignBase, a collection of geometric signs on Paleolithic mobile objects
results.reason: Verified via Crossref: Dutkiewicz et al. (2020, Sci. Data 7:364, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00704-x) describes the SignBase dataset.

results.claim: Bentz et al. (2020) is the SignBase main data file citation
results.reason: Verified: Bentz et al. (2020) is the figshare dataset citation (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.12000018.v1) for SignBase v1.0 main data file.
